vignette:
Thomas Kapoor: Six Years After

Thomas sits in the chair with his hands folded in his lap, a habit he's developed over the years-keeping them where he can see them, where they feel contained. At sixty-four, his face carries the weathered look of someone who has spent decades in warehouse work, but his eyes hold something else: a wariness that doesn't quite match his gentle demeanor.

He was fifty-eight when it happened. A routine delivery run to a commercial property in an industrial area. Three men with a gun forced him into a storage unit. They wanted money, thought he was carrying cash from the business. He wasn't. They kept him there for fourteen hours in the dark, bound to a metal chair. He doesn't talk much about what they said or did during those hours, only that time moved differently-minutes stretched like hours, and he kept thinking about his wife Priya, wondering if she'd called the police yet, if anyone was looking.

When he was finally released-the police had traced his truck-Thomas walked out into the sunlight and felt nothing. Not relief. Not joy. Just a kind of emptiness that has never quite filled in.

For the first year, he tried to return to work. Priya encouraged it. His supervisor was sympathetic. But the warehouse changed. The metal shelving that used to be simply functional now felt like it was closing in. The sound of the loading dock door slamming made his chest tighten. He'd find himself checking the exits, counting the people around him, his shoulders tensed in anticipation of something he couldn't name. After six months, he took medical leave.

Now, six years later, Thomas has never gone back. Some days he tells himself it's just practical-he's older now, his nerves aren't what they were-but both he and Priya know the truth. The thought of being in an enclosed space where he can't see the exits sends his heart racing. He's stopped going to the grocery store because the narrow aisles between shelves trigger that same suffocating sensation. He's missed his daughter's wedding reception because it was held in a banquet hall with only two doors.

The nightmares come three or four times a week. He wakes gasping, his body drenched in sweat, convinced he's still in that storage unit. Priya lies beside him, patient but tired. She's learned not to touch him when he wakes-it startles him further. He spends the rest of the night on the couch, his mind replaying scenarios: what if they had hurt him, what if no one had found him, what if, what if.

During the day, Thomas moves through their house like a ghost. He's gained weight from inactivity and lost interest in things that once brought him joy-he hasn't played cricket with his friends in years. He drinks more than he used to, usually in the evenings, telling himself it helps him sleep. It doesn't, not really, but it dulls the edge of the constant vigilance he carries.

Priya suggested therapy last year. Thomas resisted. What could talking do? But something in her voice-a kind of quiet desperation-made him reconsider. Now he sits in this office, trying to find words for something that lives deeper than language. He knows he's trapped in a way that has nothing to do with locked doors anymore. The real prison is inside him, and he's not sure anyone can help him leave.
